Analysis Pipeline: 1) Per-row median subtraction on the physically-scaled float height image (line-by-line leveling), then verify horizontal streaks over featureless regions are visibly suppressed via a fast-scan line profile; escalate to per-row 1st/2nd-order polynomial if residual stripes remain. 2) Resample to square pixels using metadata FOV (index 1: 256x512 -> 512x512); record nm/px and confirm it matches FOV_x/Nx and FOV_y/Ny within float tolerance; preserve physical height mapping (round-trip check). 3) resolve_pixel_size_nm(metadata, shape) with None-guard. 4) NYQUIST GATE: compute the finest resolvable d = 2*pixel_size_nm. If 2*pixel_size_nm > lower bound of the intended d_range, the ~0.5 nm mica lattice is physically unresolvable at this sampling -> record 'lattice unresolvable at this pixel size' and do NOT run the sub-nm reflection search (any positive result would be artifact). 5) If the pixel size DOES resolve the band, run fourier_reflection_map(image, pixel_size_nm, params) with d_range adapted to the actual resolvable range; verify the detected reflection is NOT collinear with the fast-scan/streak direction before accepting it as a real lattice. 6) In ALL cases, characterize the scale-appropriate surface/adsorbate structure to answer the objective: full-image FFT / radial power spectral density to detect any dominant periodicity or characteristic length, autocorrelation correlation length, RMS roughness (Rq) in nm, and blob/patch coverage statistics — so the 2mM vs 10mM structural change is quantified even when the sub-nm lattice is absent.

Quality Status: All analyses acceptable

1. Scientific Analysis

This series was designed to characterize how the mica surface structure and adsorbate pattern change between 2 mM and 10 mM KCl, but in practice only the 2 mM image (index 0) produced a successful, quality-approved analysis (score 0.75). The 10 mM image analysis was not successful, so the intended cross-concentration comparison could not actually be performed on measured data—every '10 mM' point rendered in the trend dashboard is a placeholder/red-X (invalid or missing), not an observation. This is critical: the plotted 'trend lines' connecting 2 mM to 10 mM are extrapolations or invalid-point overlays, not evidence of a real concentration-dependent change. For the one valid image (2 mM KCl), the analysis returned an internally coherent picture of a nanotextured mica surface imaged in electrolyte. Adsorbate/patch coverage was ~0.44 (fractional), with 313 discrete patches of mean size ~0.53 nm and a noise-gated autocorrelation correlation length of ~0.86 nm (~22 px, not noise-flagged). A radial PSD split identified a low-frequency envelope on the order of ~10 nm and a mid-frequency corrugation peak at a wavelength of ~0.67 nm. These sub-nanometer length scales are consistent with atomic/near-atomic lattice-scale corrugation of mica (0.5 mica lattice constant) plus a longer-range height envelope from ordered ions/hydration layers. Importantly, the Fourier reflection map returned a legitimate null (reflection_null_flag = true, 0 reflections detected), and sub-nm reflection detection was NOT authorized because the pixel size was assumed via an FOV fallback (assumed_fov_20nm). Thus no verified periodic lattice reflections were extracted. A dominant caveat pervades every quantitative statement: the pixel size / field of view was NOT recovered from metadata and was assumed to be 20 nm FOV (scale_uncertain_flag = true, pixel_size_source = 'assumed_fov_20nm_fallback'). Consequently all absolute length scales (correlation length, patch size, corrugation wavelength, envelope length) are only accurate up to the true-FOV scaling factor, and cross_conc validity flags for both scale and Rq are False. The Rq value (~3012) is reported in uncalibrated z-units (Rq_z_calibrated = false), so it carries no physical roughness meaning and cannot be compared across images. Given these limitations, the analysis supports a characterization of the 2 mM surface texture in relative terms but cannot yet answer the core objective of how structure evolves from 2 mM to 10 mM.

5. Scientific Claims

Claim 1: At 2 mM KCl, the mica surface in electrolyte exhibits a nanoscale patchy adsorbate/hydration texture with ~44% fractional coverage, ~0.5-0.9 nm characteristic patch/correlation length scales, and a mid-frequency height corrugation at ~0.67 nm wavelength, consistent with lattice-scale/hydration-layer ordering (subject to an unresolved absolute-scale calibration).

Scientific Impact: Quantifying sub-nanometer adsorbate/hydration structure on mica in dilute KCl constrains models of ion-specific interfacial hydration and electrical double-layer structure at solid-liquid interfaces, which underpin colloid stability, clay swelling, and nanofluidic transport.

Literature Search Query: Has anyone quantified the coverage and sub-nanometer correlation length of ordered ion/hydration structures on mica in 2 mM KCl and related the mid-frequency corrugation wavelength to the mica lattice or hydration-layer spacing?

Keywords: mica, KCl, hydration layer, AFM, correlation length, surface corrugation, electrical double layer

6. Caveats & Limitations

The dominant limitation is that only 1 of 2 images produced a valid analysis, so the intended 2 mM vs 10 mM comparison cannot be made from measured data—the 10 mM 'points' in the dashboard are invalid placeholders and any drawn regression line is not supported by observations. All absolute length scales for the 2 mM image are uncertain because pixel size/FOV was assumed via a 20 nm fallback (scale_uncertain_flag = true; scale_valid_for_cross_conc = false), meaning correlation length, patch size, envelope length, and corrugation wavelength are correct only up to an unknown scaling factor. Rq is in uncalibrated z-units (Rq_z_calibrated = false) and is not physically interpretable or comparable. The Fourier reflection map returned a legitimate null with sub-nm detection unauthorized, so no verified lattice periodicity was established. Finally, with a single valid image and no replicates, any relationship to KCl concentration is unconstrained; conclusions should be restricted to a relative characterization of the 2 mM surface texture until scale/z-calibration are recovered and the 10 mM image is successfully analyzed.
